title: Is AI Really That Scary? Where to Begin with Using AI to Support Teaching 2025
author: James Crane
source: Class Teaching, Durrington Research School (classteaching.wordpress.com), January 28,
summary: James Crane of Durrington Research School documents a concrete case study of Shane Borrett, Head of Maths at Durrington High School, using ChatGPT to speed up a time-consuming vocabulary-instruction task. Following an annual department review that flagged vocabulary as a priority, Borrett needed to produce phonetic breakdowns, child-friendly definitions, examples, non-examples, and comprehension questions for a minimum of 135 key stage 3 maths terms -- a workload Crane frames as exactly the kind of time cost that makes such good instructional ideas hard to actually implement. Crane walks through Borrett's simple process: choosing ChatGPT, writing a specific structured prompt for one word ('quadratic'), and getting a usable first draft in seconds that needed only light editing. He references an EEF trial showing that using ChatGPT alongside a teacher's guide can cut lesson-planning time by over 30%, and describes how Borrett then modelled the process for his department in a subject-specific CPD session before planning a full departmental rollout across all 135 target words.
points: Crane's framing explicitly favours 'concrete examples of how teachers use AI to do their jobs quicker or better' over abstract AI hype, grounding the whole piece in a single real workload problem (135 vocabulary terms) rather than a general AI-in-schools argument.

Borrett's exact ChatGPT prompt -- specifying phonetic breakdown, child-friendly definition, two examples, two non-examples, and comprehension questions in one request -- is a reusable, concrete template other departments could adapt directly.

The EEF trial citation (AI alongside a teacher's guide cutting lesson-planning time by over 30%) supplies independent evidence behind the anecdote, distinguishing this from a purely enthusiast case study.

Crane's own admitted 'fear and concern' reaction to AI, contrasted with Borrett's pragmatic time-saving framing, models two realistic teacher starting points and shows how a low-stakes, narrow use case (vocabulary resource generation) can shift scepticism toward adoption.
quotes: If we were granted one wish as educators, a lot of us would wish for more time.
The EEF have carried out a trial looking at the impact of AI on secondary school teachers’ planning/workload in the UK. The results are really promising.
That is a minimum of 135 keywords that the maths department would need the phonetic breakdown of, a student friendly explanation, examples, non-examples and questions to check understanding.
Now if you are like me, the thought of using a new form of technology would make you fill you with dread.
Although this isn't perfect (perhaps I should have used the term "quadratic expression") given the time it takes to make these resources I think it's a really good starting point.
After discussing the use of AI to support explicit vocabulary instruction with Shane and the ease of the process I then decided to dig a little deeper into the world of AI and teaching.
